source: Madrian and Shea (2001) The power of suggestion: inertia in 401(k) participation and savings behavior (NBER w7682, May 2000 version)
finding: A large US firm switched new hires from opt-in to automatic enrolment at 401(k). Participation jumped. The ones hired just before the switch were far less likely to join.
numbers: At 3-15 months of tenure: 37% participation (pre-switch WINDOW cohort) vs 86% (auto-enrolled NEW cohort). Firm-wide participation before the change was 61%. Observational before/after cohort comparison, one firm.
quote: 401(k) participation is significantly higher under automatic enrollment.
limits: Not randomised; one firm; the paper notes eligibility timing also changed (immediate eligibility) and says that explains little of the gap.
agent_relevance: A default can move a binary take-it-or-leave-it choice by about 49 points. Test whether our agent's pre-filled option (S0 gate default, a draft answer shown first) is accepted at a similar inflated rate.

source: Madrian and Shea (2001) The power of suggestion: inertia in 401(k) participation and savings behavior (NBER w7682, May 2000 version)
finding: The default also sets the amount and the fund. Most auto-enrolled people stayed at the company's default contribution rate and fund, which few earlier hires would have picked. With time many moved away.
numbers: 76% of NEW-cohort participants contributed at the default 3% (about 10% in other cohorts). 61% of the NEW cohort sat at the full default (participate, 3%, 100% money market); only 1% of earlier cohorts did. Non-default participation under auto-enrolment rose from 7% to 37% over the first 15 months. 86% did not opt out.
limits: Authors give two causes, inertia and 'default as advice'; they cannot separate them. A default can be harmful: it anchors a low saving rate (3%) below what earlier hires chose (6%+).
agent_relevance: Two lessons. (1) A default is both a nudge and an anchor on magnitude, so a default value in a prompt will pull estimates. (2) The pull decays with time and deliberation, so an extra review step (S7) should reduce it.

source: White, Jiang and Albarracin (2021) The limits of defaults: the influence of decision time on default effects (Social Cognition 39(5))
finding: Defaults work mainly when people decide fast. With more decision time the default advantage becomes trivial or zero. Four experiments (one preregistered, nationally representative) plus a meta-analysis.
numbers: Exp 1 N=122; Exp 2 N=119 (at 2 s: action default 73% vs no-action 31%; longer: 50% vs 57%, p=.605); Exp 3 N=222 (2 s: 86% vs 32%; longer 74% vs 57%, p=.064); Exp 4 N=637 preregistered (short time 86% vs 66%; long time 66% vs 64%, p=.506). Mini meta-analysis N=2,359, interaction d=1.19 [1.06, 1.32].
quote: short decision times increased the advantage of action defaults
limits: Charity-donation task; decision time was manipulated or measured, so slow deciders may differ in other ways in Exp 1. Online samples.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition that matters for an LLM scaffold: a default is strongest under fast, low-deliberation answering. Reasoning steps or a forced second look should shrink default and anchor pull; test it with and without a reasoning budget.

source: Jachimowicz, Duncan, Weber and Johnson (2019) When and why defaults influence decisions: a meta-analysis of default effects (Behavioural Public Policy 3(2))
finding: Pooled default effect is medium to large but varies a lot. A few studies show no effect and two show negative effects. Defaults work better when read as an endorsement or the status quo, better in consumer than in environmental domains.
numbers: 58 studies, pooled n=73,675, d=0.68 (95% CI 0.53 to 0.83). Only the abstract record was opened (RePEc and a web summary); moderator sizes and publication-bias tests were not read.
limits: Abstract level only. This meta-analysis predates and is not corrected by the Maier et al. 2022 RoBMA approach; Maier's 'structure' category (which includes defaults) fell to 0.12 [0.00, 0.43] after correction, so d=0.68 is probably inflated by publication bias. No direct corrected estimate for defaults alone was found.
agent_relevance: Use d about 0.7 as an upper bound, and plan for a smaller true default pull. The endorsement mechanism matters: an LLM may treat a pre-filled option as a recommendation, which is the large-effect route.

source: Aleksovska, Schillemans and Grimmelikhuijsen (2019) Lessons from five decades of experimental and behavioral research on accountability: a systematic literature review (J Behavioral Public Administration 2(2))
finding: Systematic review of accountability experiments. Accountability mostly raises effort and information processing and mostly weakens biases, with exceptions. Telling people before they see the task works better than after. Process accountability gives more thought-through, calibrated, consistent decisions; outcome accountability gives more commitment and sometimes better performance.
numbers: 266 experiments in 211 articles, 1970-2016. Findings are vote-count summaries (scores from -1 to 1 per relationship), not pooled effect sizes. Effects tested in at least 5 experiments: more information searched, deeper processing, more time and effort. Dilution effect is made worse by accountability. Accountability lowers confidence and overconfidence and raises caution and defensive behaviour.
quote: setting an accountability expectation before any element of the task is presented, results in less biased decisions
limits: No effect sizes. Most bias effects rest on one or a few studies. Humans answering to a real audience, so it may not carry over to a prompt line.
agent_relevance: Supports 'accountability before the task, for process' as a scaffold feature: state at S0 that the reasoning will be audited step by step. Expect more caution and less overconfidence, and expect a dilution-type cost (irrelevant facts get used).

source: Lerner and Tetlock (1999) Accounting for the effects of accountability (Psychological Bulletin 125(2):255-275)
finding: Abstract only: the review asks how accountability rules shape thinking, when accountability weakens, ignores or strengthens bias, whether it changes thought or only what is said, and what goals accountable people pursue.
numbers: No numbers retrieved. Full text was paywalled (403 on APA, Harvard and other mirrors tried). Claims often attributed to this paper (pre-exposure accountability to an unknown audience, process over outcome, exploratory vs confirmatory thought) were seen here only through the Aleksovska review (d05).
limits: Gap 2 stays partly open: no effect sizes for specific biases. Abstract was paraphrased by the fetch tool; no verbatim quote.
agent_relevance: Same as d05. The key design point from the abstract is that accountability can strengthen bias when the audience's view is known (people conform), so an agent prompt should name an accuracy-demanding audience with unknown views.

source: Bucinca, Malaya and Gajos (2021) To trust or to think: cognitive forcing functions can reduce overreliance on AI in AI-assisted decision-making (CSCW)
finding: Forcing people to think before seeing the AI answer (wait) or to ask for it (on demand) reduced following wrong AI advice, compared with plain explanations. But teams still did worse than the AI alone, and people disliked the forcing designs most.
numbers: N=199 on Mechanical Turk, nutrition task, simulated AI with 75% accuracy; chi-square on incorrect-AI trials N=663: overall chi2(2)=13.30, p=.0013; carb-source chi2(2)=44.35, p<.0001. Cognitive forcing lowered overreliance significantly on carb-source detection, not significantly overall; no gain in overall team performance (H1b not supported).
limits: Simulated AI, one task, MTurk. Benefits larger for people high in Need for Cognition, so it can widen inequality.
agent_relevance: A forced-choice step before the model sees its own or a retrieved answer (commit to a first estimate, then compare with the class record) is the structural analogue. Expect smaller gains than hoped, and a usability cost.

source: Vasconcelos et al. (2023) Explanations can reduce overreliance on AI systems during decision-making (CSCW)
finding: Overreliance on AI advice is a cost-benefit choice. It falls when the task is hard and the explanation makes checking cheap. It does not fall when the task is easy, which explains earlier null results.
numbers: Five studies, N=731 total, maze task with a simulated AI. Highlight explanations reduced overreliance in the hard task (Table 5 contrast Prediction-Highlight 2.47 [1.72, 3.36] on the model scale).
limits: Simulated AI in a maze; effect sizes are on a Bayesian mixed-model scale, not percentages.
agent_relevance: Over-reliance on an advisory signal (a retrieved base rate, a prior answer) is strategic. A cheap-to-check base rate gets used; a hard-to-check one gets ignored or copied blindly.

source: Vasconcelos et al. (2023) Explanations can reduce overreliance on AI systems during decision-making, Study 4 (bonus)
finding: Paying more for a correct final answer lowered overreliance on a wrong AI. A direct incentive effect on a bias-like behaviour.
numbers: Study 4 N=114; low bonus $0.01 vs high bonus $0.50 per correct maze; posterior mean difference 0.93 [0.41, 1.46] (credible interval excludes 0), overreliance lower with high bonus.
limits: Small sample, one task, simulated AI; incentive sizes were 50 times apart, so this does not give a dose-response.
agent_relevance: Analogy only: for an LLM, a stated reward has no real cost, so this human effect cannot be assumed to transfer. It supports testing a stakes or penalty line, with calibration measured.

source: Echterhoff, Liu, Alessa, McAuley and He (2024) Cognitive bias in decision-making with LLMs (BiasBuster, Findings EMNLP)
finding: Asked models to debias. Awareness helped Llama anchoring a bit; few-shot and counterfactual prompts often broke instruction following. The self-help method (model rewrites its own biased prompt) worked best, mostly on larger models.
numbers: 13,465 prompts; models GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4, Llama 2 7B and 13B. GPT-4 admitted 40.5% more students under the reject framing; Llama 2 7B called 32.1% fewer females good at math. Self-help cut biased prompt elements to 0% for group attribution in GPT-4, 2.7% for framing; GPT-3.5 reduced group-attribution prompts by only 8.9%, framing/status quo to 17.2% and 8.5%. Llama models changed 40 to 52% of anchoring decisions between sequential and self-help setup.
limits: 2023 models. Success counted as removed bias-inducing words, not as better final accuracy. Few-shot sometimes pushed probability to 0 or 1.
agent_relevance: A structural rewrite (strip the anchor, re-ask with all facts at once) beat a warning line and beat examples; matches gap 7. Needs capable models; test on current ones.

source: Sumita, Takeuchi and Kashima (2024) Cognitive biases in large language models: a survey and mitigation experiments (arXiv 2412.00323; SAC 2025)
finding: Authors of the arXiv 2412 paper previously unattributed in our notes (b17). On six evaluator biases in GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, awareness reminders helped several biases; social-projection prompting (answer as most people would) made the bandwagon effect much worse.
numbers: CoBBLEr benchmark, six biases. AwaRe: effective on GPT-3.5 for order, compassion fade, egocentric, bandwagon, attentional; on GPT-4 for bandwagon and verbosity. SoPro 'significantly worsens' bandwagon, helps egocentric in GPT-3.5 and verbosity in GPT-4. Order bias: no significant change from any method in either model (as stated in the order-bias paragraph, which says no significant change for either model from the existing method or the new ones).
limits: Reported as colour-coded score tables with qualitative reading; two models only; evaluator-task biases, not forecasting. The discussion text also credits AwaRe with an order-bias gain on GPT-3.5, which conflicts with the results paragraph; treat order-bias effect as unclear.
agent_relevance: Warning lines are model-specific and can fail. A 'think like the majority' step imports conformity; do not use it for the outside-view step unless the class record is data, not opinion.

source: Malberg, Poletukhin, Schuster and Groh (2024) A comprehensive evaluation of cognitive biases in LLMs (arXiv 2410.15413)
finding: 30 biases, 20 models, 30,000 tests. All 30 biases appear in some model. Average bias scores: anchoring 0.39, framing 0.41, optimism bias 0.06; status-quo bias is strongly negative (-0.42), meaning models prefer change.
numbers: 20 LLMs (e.g. GPT-4o, Llama 3.1, Claude 3 Haiku, Gemini 1.5, Qwen2.5 72B) plus a random baseline. Anchoring by model ranged -0.05 to 0.67 (GPT-4o 0.60, Claude 3 Haiku 0.67, Llama 3.1 70B 0.64). Framing 0.10 to 0.55. Averages read from the paper's heatmap table.
limits: Frontier models of mid 2024. Bias scores are control-vs-treatment shifts on prompt templates, not accuracy. Smallest Llama (1B) looks unbiased only because it often fails to decide (33%).
agent_relevance: Size does not remove anchoring or framing in 2024 models; the structural fix must be in the scaffold. Status quo goes the other way, so a default in the prompt may be under-followed by an LLM; test its sign.

source: Malberg et al. (2024) A comprehensive evaluation of cognitive biases in LLMs, planning-fallacy test (appendix B.26)
finding: Direct test of whether a model keeps an optimistic time plan after being told the reference class overran. Most models update about enough or too much (planning fallacy score near 0 or negative).
numbers: Score per model: GPT-4o -0.16, GPT-4o mini -0.06, GPT-3.5 -0.04, Llama 3.1 405B -0.02, Llama 3.2 3B 0.19, Llama 3.2 1B 0.20, Gemini 1.5 Pro -0.14, Gemma 2 27B -0.17; average about -0.02. Design: control asks for time to allocate; treatment adds the percentage of overdue time on similar projects.
limits: Single-template test of belief updating, not of forecast accuracy; the true outcome is not known. Does not test whether the model retrieves a good class by itself. Column-to-model mapping was parsed from a flattened PDF table; verify before quoting single cells.
agent_relevance: Partly closes gap 1: when handed the class overrun rate, current-generation LLMs use it. The weak step is picking and retrieving the class, not applying it. Test that step.

source: Planning fallacy (secondary summary of Buehler, Griffin and Ross 1994 and later work; Wikipedia, read this session)
finding: Secondary source for the founding planning-fallacy numbers. Students expected 33.9 days for their thesis, took 55.5. About 30% finished by their own estimate. Personal-project study: 13% finished by the 50% estimate, 19% by the 75% estimate, 45% by the 99% estimate.
numbers: Thesis study mean predicted 33.9, best case 27.4, worst case 48.6 days, actual 55.5 days. Observers over-estimate others' time (pessimistic bias). Implementation intentions and segmentation cut the bias in single studies; the page gives no outside-view experiment numbers.
limits: SECONDARY SOURCE: primary Buehler 1994 and Buehler 2010 chapter were paywalled and not opened. Wikipedia gives no preregistered outside-view test.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 stays open for the effect of the outside-view prompt. The numbers give the size of the bias a class-based correction must fix: a plan hits its own best-case time under a third of the time.

source: Leleur, Salling, Pilkauskiene and Nicolaisen (2015) Combining reference class forecasting with overconfidence theory for better risk assessment of transport infrastructure investments (EJTIR 15(3))
finding: Proposes a flexible RCF: build the best reference pool and use overconfidence theory to read expert estimates. Treats class choice as the weak point of RCF.
numbers: No numbers on the page read (abstract only). UNITE database 2009-2013, count not stated.
limits: Abstract only. Methodological proposal, not a replication or failure test. Does not close gap 9.
agent_relevance: Class choice is the leverage point: an agent's class record must be selected by similarity, with an overconfidence adjustment on the agent's own estimate.

source: Lovallo, Clarke and Camerer (2012) Robust analogizing and the outside view: two empirical tests of case-based decision making (Strategic Management Journal)
finding: Found in Crossref only; full text and abstract fetch returned 403. Title says it tests case-based (analogy) forecasting empirically in two studies.
limits: Not opened. Cannot be quoted. It is the best candidate for a non-infrastructure test of the outside view (gap 9) and should be read next.
agent_relevance: Candidate source for 'how selective analogy hurts the outside view'.

source: Tian et al. (2023) Just ask for calibration: strategies for eliciting calibrated confidence scores from RLHF language models (EMNLP)
finding: Verbalised confidence from RLHF models is better calibrated than their token probabilities. Relevant to measuring calibration (gap 10), not to incentives.
numbers: Expected calibration error cut by a relative 50% or so on TriviaQA, SciQ and TruthfulQA for ChatGPT, GPT-4 and Claude (abstract level).
limits: Abstract only. No incentive or accountability manipulation. Gap 10 stays open: no study found that changes the stakes or audience line and measures calibration.
agent_relevance: If we test a stakes line we should measure calibration with verbalised confidence, as this paper supports.
